match.reason: The closest point, supply-side policies, is broader and covers many policies, while labour market reform and enterprise bargaining is a narrower idea that needs its own point.

draft.title: Labour market reform
card: The labour market is where workers sell their labour and employers buy it. Labour market reform changes the rules for how wages and conditions are set.
wages and conditions were set for whole industries or occupations by a tribunal, through awards. Firms had little say over their own pay and work practices.
wages and conditions are agreed between an employer and its employees at the workplace. This became the main way of setting pay in Australia from the 1990s.
The aim is a more flexible labour market, where pay and work practices can suit each firm. Supporters argue this lifts labour productivity, which is output per worker, and so helps long-term growth.
draft.remember: Labour market reform moves pay-setting closer to the workplace, aiming for flexibility and higher productivity.

a.q: Which change is an example of labour market reform in Australia?
opts: Moving from industry-wide awards to enterprise bargaining
Raising the tax paid on goods and services
Banning firms from agreeing to fix their prices
Cutting tariffs on imported cars
a.why: Enterprise bargaining changes how wages and conditions are set, which is labour market reform. Banning price fixing is competition policy, not a change to how pay is set.
a.clue: Look for the change to how pay and conditions are decided.

b.q: Dev runs a bakery chain in Perth. Under enterprise bargaining, he agrees new rosters and pay with his staff. Why might this raise productivity?
opts: Work practices can be fitted to the needs of his bakeries
A tribunal sets one pay rate for every bakery in Australia
Workers must accept lower wages in every bakery
The government sets the number of staff each bakery hires
b.why: Enterprise bargaining lets the employer and staff agree on arrangements that suit their own workplace, which aims to lift output per worker. A single rate set by a tribunal describes the older centralised system, so it is the tempting wrong answer.
b.clue: Think about who now decides the arrangements, and how close they are to the work.

a.best: Moving from industry-wide awards to enterprise bargaining

b.best: Work practices can be fitted to the needs of his bakeries

problems.detail: The card puts awards only in the past tense ('were set ... through awards'), which suggests awards no longer exist. Modern awards still operate under the Fair Work Act as a safety net and still directly cover a sizeable share of workers. Saying enterprise bargaining is 'the main way' of setting pay also oversimplifies, since individual arrangements cover a similar share of employees.
The distractor 'Workers must accept lower wages in every bakery' uses 'must', an absolute the card does not support. This makes it easy to rule out without knowing the idea.

check.summary: Both questions work and have one clear right answer. The card's past-tense account of awards could suggest they no longer exist, when modern awards remain a safety net, and one distractor uses an absolute 'must'.

proposal.title: Labour market reform
card: The labour market is where workers sell their labour and employers buy it. Labour market reform changes the rules for how wages and conditions are set.
a tribunal set wages and conditions for whole industries or occupations through awards. Before the 1990s, most firms had little say over their own pay and work practices.

an employer and its employees agree wages and conditions at the workplace. It spread widely from the 1990s, while modern awards remain under the Fair Work Act as a safety net of minimum pay and conditions.
The aim is a more flexible labour market, where pay and work practices can suit each firm. Supporters argue this lifts labour productivity, which is output per worker, and so helps long-term growth.
proposal.remember: Labour market reform moves more pay-setting closer to the workplace, aiming for flexibility and higher productivity.

a.q: Which change is an example of labour market reform in Australia?
opts: Moving from industry-wide awards to enterprise bargaining
Raising the tax paid on goods and services
Banning firms from agreeing to fix their prices
Cutting tariffs on imported cars
a.why: Enterprise bargaining changes how wages and conditions are set, which is labour market reform. Banning price fixing is competition policy, not a change to how pay is set.
a.clue: Look for the change to how pay and conditions are decided.

b.q: Dev runs a bakery chain in Perth. Under enterprise bargaining, he agrees new rosters and pay with his staff. Why might this raise productivity?
opts: Work practices can be fitted to the needs of his bakeries
A tribunal sets one pay rate for every bakery in Australia
Staff earn less, so the bakeries' wage bill falls
The government sets the number of staff each bakery hires
b.why: Enterprise bargaining lets the employer and staff agree on arrangements that suit their own workplace, which aims to lift output per worker. A single rate set by a tribunal describes the centralised system, and a lower wage bill cuts costs but does not raise output per worker.
